Call of Duty: MW4 Promo Features Akash Missile
articles.text:
India’s home-grown Akash surface-to-air missile system has seen the interest of defence buff and gamers after a viral video which supposedly showed an Akash missile in the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 has sparked debate about the possible appearance of an Indian air defence system in the latest instalment of the military shooter franchise.
The footage has been shared by users commenting on the game’s campaign, indicating the presence of a system which they believe to be the Akash missile system. However, the identity of the system shown in the footage has not been confirmed by the game’s developers, and its appearance should be regarded as a mere identification from a visual standpoint, not an official confirmation of the inclusion of the Indian weapon.
Designed by the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), Akash is a mobile, short-range surface-to-air missile system, made with the purpose of protecting vulnerable places and installations from aerial attacks. It can simultaneously attack more than one target in group or autonomous modes, and features electronic counter-countermeasures to improve its resistance in contested electromagnetic environments. It has been deployed with the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force.
Akash is an important example of India’s commitment to developing indigenous air defence systems. The system features missile launchers, along with radar and command-and-control components, allowing it to detect, track and engage incoming aerial threats. DRDO has worked on developing and upgrading the Akash family of missiles, while Indian defence manufacturers can assist in producing the system and its related equipment.
The appearance in Modern Warfare 4 is of particular significance, given that military video games often feature real-life weapons, vehicles and equipment, utilised to recreate identifiable combat environments. Nevertheless, their presence in such games is typically inspired by the use of their real-life counterparts, which are adapted for presentation within the context of the game’s ruleset, and a mere visual similarity is not sufficient to assert that a given weapon has been recreated in a specific game.
The game’s website advertises a fictional war, which takes place around an invasion of the Korean Peninsula, with campaign locations including several international settings. While its developers have advertised the title around its cinematic combat and detailed weapon handling, the provided information does not address the appearance of the suspected Akash sequence.
Akash would bring an Indian-made air defence system into the fold of a major gaming franchise, potentially exposing the system to a new audience. However, a single appearance in a game would not be sufficient to indicate that an official partnership, endorsement or effort to promote Indian defence technology has taken place.

articles.title: Arc browser on its way out as makers suggest an alternative
articles.text:
The Arc browser has flatlined, with its maker announcing it will be sunsetting it altogether on December 22, 2026. The Browser Company announced the news on October 22, just over three years after we noted Arc's arrival.

Nothing will happen immediately, other than an end to new Arc accounts. Starting November 23, lights will begin turning off on iOS and Android, with several AI features disabled and sign-ins to sync tabs removed. Finally, on December 22, it will no longer be possible to access or use Arc on macOS and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and data deleted within 30 days.

The solution? According to The Browser Company, a move to its AI browser, Dia, is one way forward. Users can import their profiles into the brave, new AI-native world and carry on as before. Sort of.

When it launched, the Chromium-based Arc was an innovative browser with a workflow unlike its rivals. Instead of a plethora of tabs, there was a sidebar. The browser attempted to change how users interacted with the web but… frankly… it never really caught on.

The writing was on the wall for a while. In 2025, The Browser Company pivoted to AI and its Dia browser, dropping Arc into maintenance mode. Later that year, the vendor was snapped up by Atlassian, although Arc continued to plow its lonely furrow.

However, a year on, the time has come for Arc. CEO Josh Miller wrote: "We have so much pride and love for what we made alongside the Arc community," but it seems that wasn't enough to keep the browser maintained alongside Dia development.

Hopes that Arc might be open-sourced so that its community could continue development were dashed in 2025, when Miller explained that "Arc isn't just a Chromium fork … It runs on custom infrastructure we call ADK — the Arc Development Kit."

Dia also uses ADK.

Arc's innovations have found their way, at least in part, into other browsers. Many users have found solace in the Zen browser, and there is always Vivaldi for power users. There is also a level of risk in going all-in on AI-native browsers in an increasingly crowded marketplace. For example, Strawberry, currently in beta, leverages AI agents to smooth a user's workflow. Dia might be a successor to Arc, but there is a risk that users will consider something else.

As for Arc itself, The Browser Company plans to focus on Dia going forward. So for the Arc community, it is time to move on. ®

articles.title: India May Need 35–45 SSNs for Two-Sea Denial, Simulation Finds
articles.text:
India would require a fleet of between 35 and 45 nuclear-powered attack submarines (SSNs) to maintain sea denial across six maritime barriers in a hypothetical two-front war with China and Pakistan, an in-house simulation suggests. In the illustrative example, the authors estimate that the six-boat SSN programme described in the study would offer a limited denial capability rather than continuous coverage of the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal and wider Indian Ocean access points.
The Python-based simulation calculates the availability of the force over time and the number of boats required to maintain pickets across multiple barriers. It assumes a duty-cycle model in which each submarine spends 100 days in maintenance and work-up, six days transiting to and from their operating station and 75 days on patrol: a 41.4 per cent duty cycle on average, given the time spent in transit.
This has a significant impact on the force size needed to maintain pickets on a sustained basis. A six-boat force averages roughly two submarines on station, compared to five in a 12-boat fleet. The model estimates that maintaining 15 stations would require 37 submarines on an expected-value basis, and more than 40 when using a more demanding probabilistic method.
The second part of the simulation uses a simplifed barrier model to calculate the probability of detecting a transiting vessel. Each submarine is assumed to detect traffic within 40 nautical miles either side, giving a nominal 80-nautical mile wide picket on either side of a barrier. The calculation assumes each ship passes through once, without escort, and does not consider speed, evasion or altered routing.
In this case, a six-SSN fleet fully covers one barrier, with a width-weighted detection probability of 0.15 across the modelled barriers. A 12-boat force covers three barriers, with a detection probability of 0.32, and 18 submarines covers four with a probability of 0.46, while a 30-boat fleet covers five with a probability of 0.78.
The model calculates full coverage of all six barriers as 36 submarines on average, with a width-weighted detection probability of 1.00 under these assumptions. However, this should not be taken to mean that every vessel would be detected: this is a consequence of the way the model is structured, and does not reflect reality.
The study groups the potential force requirement into three broad categories. A limited sea denial force of around eight to 12 SSNs would concentrate on two high-value approaches – defined in the model as the western Malacca approach and the Karachi-Gwadar coast – while a posture covering four or five barriers would require approximately 18 to 30 boats, and continuous picketing across all six would require a much larger fleet.
For India, the main conclusion from the study is the gap between the proposed six-boat programme and the force size required to maintain persistent coverage. The authors suggest that conventional submarines, P-8I maritime patrol aircraft, mines and unmanned systems could contribute to a layered approach, leaving SSNs to focus on open-ocean operations and other high-value missions.
The authors note that merchant traffic can take alternate routes through the Sunda and Lombok straits or via open-ocean routes, and that the results are sensitive to assumptions about detection range and barrier width, as well as the availability of SSNs. Halving the assumed detection range would roughly double the picket requirement.

articles.title: SparkyOS: Lightweight general-purpose Arch, on a pendrive
articles.text:
SparkyOS is a novel distro from the folks behind SparkyLinux: it's a version of Arch that can you can use without installing it at all.

SparkyOS is a new distro from the team behind the Debian-based SparkyLinux, but it's quite different. SparkyOS is based on Arch, and it runs entirely from USB. It's not a conventional live medium – this is a full local install, but shipped as an image of a USB key that you can boot and run. It comes with the Xfce desktop and an array of apps. The idea is that you can boot and run it on any x86-64 UEFI computer, entirely from a USB key, without touching the hard disk at all.

This is quite different from its forerunner, which is a relatively conventional Debian-based distro, one which The Register has mentioned a few times over the years: first back in 2015 in a lightweight distro roundup, and more recently in 2024 when we praised its array of desktop environments. Earlier this year, we noted that the latest SparkyLinux featured a complete 32-bit edition, even though its parent distro has dropped its 32-bit x86 kernel.

This is also not your typical live distro. Unless you're running on some Arm computer with nonstandard firmware, most Linux distros install from an image written to a USB pendrive, the same way that they did decades ago: in the noughties when they installed from a DVD, and back in the 20th century, when it was a CD instead. Most optical media use some form of the ISO standard 9660 filesystem, which is quite limited – despite multiple extensions, the core is a basic structure comparable to the ancient MS-DOS FAT. That's not much use for Linux, which needs long filenames, permissions, and metadata, plus things like symbolic links.

So, to this day, most live Linux media have a few boot files and the OS itself is kept inside a big compressed file called a SquashFS, inside which is a real Linux filesystem. However, because it's inside something akin to a Zip file, it's read-only. You can't update the OS or add new software. Some live media optionally offer persistence, which stores changes in another separate file. That works, but if you update the OS, all the original pre-update files remain untouched, and new ones are stored in the persistence structure in addition to the space still consumed by the originals. So, it's slow, and it's very inefficient; it takes substantially more space than a conventional disk install.

So, although there are dozens, maybe hundreds, of live Linux media images out there, most fall into one of two types of single-purpose product: either stripped-out special-purpose distros, such as SystemRescue, GParted Live, and Grml, or Rescuezilla, or Clonezilla. Alternatively, it's a full OS, but only meant as a sampler, not for daily use, with limited and inefficient tools for updates and changes. We're not sure if twice counts as a FAQ, but there are questions on StackExchange on how to install Ubuntu to USB as well as how to install Debian to USB.

SparkyOS is an answer to this question. It's a complete, pre-configured installation of Arch, directly onto a USB key. That does impose some limits, so for instance, like the Desktop Classic System we looked at in January, it only includes UEFI boot files. You can't use it on a computer with just a "legacy" BIOS, and it requires format conversion to use it in a VM.

The current SparkyOS version 2026.10 is the first release, but there are already some How-to documentation pages covering things like expanding the filesystem to fill the USB medium, changing its settings, and how to crowbar it into a VM. The image is 10 GB in size, compressed to 3.2 GB for download, and because this is an image of an entire key, it won't work with multiboot tools such as Reg FOSS desk favorite Ventoy. We put it onto a 64 GB key, and we chose one that has two connectors for both USB-A and USB-C ports. We tested it on our oldest UEFI box, a 15-year-old Thinkpad W520, and our newest UEFI testbed, a Dell XPS13 new enough that it only has USB-C ports.

We would suggest a USB 3 key, though, and use a blue-colored USB-A port if you have one. It will run on a USB-2 only machine, but a bit slower. We tried it on our X220, currently running OpenBSD 8.0, and it worked fine. It could even see OpenBSD’s 10 separate partitions, although not mount them. SparkyOS worked flawlessly on all three machines.

The team has made some concessions to running from USB flash media. The root volume is mounted with the noatime parameter, which stops Linux from recording the last access time on files. That dramatically lowers the number of writes to the drive. There’s also no swap configured – to our surprise, not even ZRAM, which doesn’t touch the disk.

SparkyOS does what it says: it's a complete, very usable, ready-to-run Linux OS, as fully capable of being updated, customized, and having apps added or removed as any other distro… running off a pendrive. We do suggest a big fast key, though, and don't fill it up. Flash isn't like RAM: you can't change a single byte, or word, at a time. Flash can only erase a whole block at a time, and block sizes vary from 16 kB for the smallest flash chips, up to multiple megabytes. To rewrite one byte on a flash drive, the storage controller has to copy a megabyte or more of data elsewhere, format the block, and then copy it back. So, leaving more free space on a flash drive gives the on-device storage-management chip more room to work. The more free space there is on a flash drive, the longer it will last.

This is one reason flash-based SSDs wear out – and also why we wrote that the end of Optane was bad news for the whole industry. SSDs often have multiple, high-speed flash chips on. Pendrives don't – there’s usually just one.

In a previous life, over a decade and a half ago, this vulture had a small startup company, and one of our products was a live Linux-based OS, pre-installed on bootable USB keys. I did everything I could to reduce writes to the drive: they were formatted with journalling disabled, mounted with noatime, with ZRAM for swap, the temporary-files directory kept in a RAMdisk, and more. The keys sold quite well, but one of the problems was that despite all my precautions, heavy users found that the drives simply wore out.

Flash media do not fail in the same way that industry old-timers know from spinning hard disks. A dying hard disk often struggles on, just with some blocks unreadable. That’s why tools such as GNU ddrescue exist – to try to copy the data off the regions that still work. When flash media fail, they tend to fail totally: you can't read from the device at all, meaning that nothing can be recovered from them.

An example of a fairly extreme adaptation in this direction is the FreeBSD-based XigmaNAS OS. In its Embedded installation mode on a flash drive, it writes its log files to a RAM drive to prevent wear to the flash. (The snag being that they are lost when it reboots.) A user add-on for to the proprietary unRAID NAS OS does the same.

There's room for future enhancements to SparkyOS here. Booting from both BIOS and UEFI is already on the "to do" list at the bottom of the release announcement. Additionally, steps to keep any files the OS writes to in RAM, and only write them out to flash at shutdown time, and so on.

But saying all that, it's here, it works, and it already looks like a handy tool if you regularly use multiple different computers and want to carry your own environment around with you. For routine use, though, use a big fast drive, connect it to USB-3 or USB-C ports whenever possible, and ensure it stays mostly empty — keep it under 50 percent full. Most importantly of all, regularly back up any data you keep on it. ®

articles.title: How India and Australia Could Monitor Indian Ocean Chokepoints
articles.text:
India and Australia have a strategic relationship in the eastern Indian Ocean as the Andaman and Nicobar Islands group look down on the Indian Ocean, with Australian Cocos (Keeling) Islands further south. Linking surveillance capabilities could aid patrol of maritime traffic through the Indonesian archipelago between Pacific and Indian oceans, but just how integrated the two nations’ efforts are is unclear.
India’s Andaman and Nicobar Command looks over the approaches to the Strait of Malacca, a major transit route between the Indian and Pacific oceans, while the Cocos Islands group occupies a vantage point over the Sunda and Lombok straits. The proximity of these two island groups makes them valuable for maritime domain awareness, but they cannot provide radar, signals intelligence or anti-submarine warfare coverage of the three straits simultaneously.
Australia’s proposed upgrades to Cocos airfield are key to any long-term benefit to this partnership. The improved runway would allow more heavy maritime patrol aircraft to be based there, able to stay on station for longer periods of time. The supplied material suggests the work will be completed close to 2028. Once that deadline passes, Cocos could prove to be a valuable forward operating base for RAAF aircraft.
The Boeing P-8 poses a natural opportunity for operations between the two nations. Australia owns the P-8A Poseidon while India possesses the P-8I Neptune; both are maritime patrol aircraft fitted to carry sonobuoys to detect submarines. With access to airfields, maintenance and support facilities, the range of such aircraft can be extended to allow them to linger over distant regions of ocean.
India and Australia have a Mutual Logistics Support Arrangement which provides for the support of each other’s forces. Such an agreement would facilitate the provision of services and resources required to support their respective military aircraft, but it does not confirm either nation’s P-8s will operate from the other’s territory. The use of Cocos by the Indian Navy or the use of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands by the RAAF would require specific arrangements.
China’s growing naval footprint in the Indian Ocean is a factor in the relationship. The People’s Liberation Army Navy has an interest in the sea lanes of commerce which pass through the Indonesian archipelago, including those carrying energy supplies. Surveillance of submarines transiting the straits is a major concern for nations patrolling the waters, but cooperation between India and Australia will aid awareness. However, the ability to detect or persistently track a submarine cannot be assumed solely because patrol aircraft operate from two distant islands.
The proposed upgrades to Cocos airfield would give Australia more options in maintaining its own maritime patrol aircraft while India’s location in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands gives it a look over the Malacca strait. It is unclear what impact, if any, this partnership will have on the detection of submarines, but it will depend on cooperation and the use of the enhanced facilities.

articles.title: India Reminds UN of Pakistan’s Refusal to Claim Soldiers’ Bodies During Kargil Conflict
articles.text:
India slammed Pakistan at the UN, reminding the country that it did not even accept the bodies of its own soldiers killed in combat in the 1999 Kargil war but speaks about faith, religious freedom and burials.
The interim report of the Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion and belief, Nazila Ghanea, said that “Reports of systemic denial of funeral rights in the context of individuals killed in security operations in Jammu and Kashmir, India, including denial of return of bodies to families and remote and secret burials, disproportionately affecting Muslims and notably inconsistent with their practices, raise serious concerns.” Responding to the report, First Secretary at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Bhavika Mangalanandan said here on Thursday, “It is deeply ironic that a State that did not even accept the bodies of its own soldiers who were killed in combat in 1999 in Kargil unabashedly speaks with fervour on faith, religious freedom, and burials.” Indian Army recovered bodies of Pakistani soldiers who died in the Kargil War and provided them with burials after Pakistan refused to acknowledge the involvement of Pakistan Army personnel in the war.
Addressing the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on freedom of religion and belief on the topic of funeral rights in exceptional circumstances, Mangalanandan reminded Pakistan that it was the Indian Army that buried several Pakistani soldiers with military honours and in accordance with Islamic rights.
“Pakistan’s deep obsession with what is happening in the Indian Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir should be actually directed at the developments that are underway in the parts of Jammu and Kashmir under its illegal occupation, such as Rawalakot,” she said, adding that in Pakistan, a number of minorities are shrinking; their rights regularly abused.
“A State that cannot ensure the safety of its own minorities has no standing to lecture India,” she said.
Minorities in Pakistan make up approximately 4 per cent of the total population, comprising mainly Hindus, Christians, and Sikhs.
Human Rights Commission of Pakistan (HRCP) in its seventh annual report, titled “Sanctuary Denied: Freedom of Religion or Belief in 2025/26”, released last week, said minorities in Pakistan continue to face violations of fundamental rights, misuse of blasphemy laws, forced marriages and conversions, and discriminatory practices.
Mangalanandan added that burial rights for terrorists are being justified by indicating that States may restrict funeral rights of terrorists, but only within legal limits.
“Legal limits should be determined in accordance with the principles of sovereign rights. “The report goes back half a decade to find references to my country. It fails when it comes to grave violations committed recently in our region and in the developed world,” she said.

articles.title: PubKeep picks up where Microsoft Publisher signs off
articles.text:
Microsoft ended support for Publisher this month, but users with orphaned documents still have options.

Support for perpetual versions ended on October 13, but those copies will keep working without further security updates, bug fixes, or technical support.

Publisher left Microsoft 365 subscriptions on October 1, although existing installations may remain accessible until removal updates arrive. Those start reaching Current Channel devices in mid-November and Monthly Enterprise Channel devices in early December.

Microsoft first let users know in 2024 that the venerable application would be scrapped, and the Windows behemoth offered little comfort to those who needed it. Microsoft suggested Word and PowerPoint as alternatives, but neither directly opens Publisher's .pub files.

The Document Foundation, the organization behind LibreOffice, was quick to point users toward LibreOffice Draw, which uses the libmspub library to import Publisher files and can save them in OpenDocument Format (ODF). Other alternatives aim to recreate more of the Publisher experience.

Adam Anderly, founder of Texas-based Saint Systems, created PubKeep to replace Microsoft's application. PubKeep is proprietary, with no plans to open source the code. But it doesn't require a subscription: a one-time payment of $99 buys the application.

The application runs on Windows or macOS, and a lightweight browser version is available. It looks a lot like Publisher, and can handle files from Publisher 2000 through 2021. Publisher 97 and 98 are also supported, but the files are sent to a conversion service (with the user's approval) to be converted to a newer format, so anybody worried about data leaving their local device should think carefully before opening those older files.

Anderly told The Register that the project began after users expressed alarm about losing access to decades of files because of Microsoft's plans. The first challenge was the file format itself.

He said: "Microsoft never published a spec for the .pub format. It did document some of the pieces Publisher is built on: the OLE compound file container, the document properties, and the Office Drawing records used for shapes and pictures. For everything else, we used libmspub, the Document Liberation Project's open source parser behind LibreOffice's Publisher import, as a reference.

"Our testing showed it had gaps, so we wrote our own engine in TypeScript. The same engine runs in the desktop app and in the browser. From there we built a test harness around Publisher itself. We assembled a corpus of real-world .pub files. An evaluation engine renders each file two ways, through Publisher's own PDF export and through our engine, and compares the output page by page, so every change we make is scored against Publisher."

He added: "For the parts no one had documented, we made small, controlled changes to documents in Publisher and studied how the saved files changed. A licensed perpetual copy of Publisher on a Windows machine is the reference."

Anderly emphasized: "We never decompiled or modified Publisher itself. Beyond Microsoft's published specs and libmspub, everything we learned came from the files and PDFs Publisher produces."

We took a copy for a spin and it opened every .pub file we tried, although that was hardly an exhaustive compatibility test. Anderly said the company would rapidly address problems reported by users.

Register readers will be unsurprised to know that Claude Code is involved, something that Anderly says makes responsive support possible, with agents reproducing problems and writing fixes. "Most issues are fixed the same day," said Anderly. "That leaves us time to answer every report and email personally."

Although the code is proprietary, Anderly told us: "The .pubk format we save to is open, so anything you make in PubKeep isn't locked in the way .pub files were." PubKeep describes .pubk as a documented ZIP-based format containing JSON and images. That makes its contents inspectable, although it doesn't guarantee another application can reproduce the layout.

For Publisher users seeking a familiar replacement, PubKeep offers another option. The $99 price includes a year of support.

What's more striking is how quickly a relatively small team built something that reproduces much of Publisher's functionality.

PubKeep is part of a broader reimplementation trend. Other projects are taking on applications that remain very much alive, including Word, Excel, and Photoshop. ®

The Squadron That Never Was: How India’s Bid for 21 Russian Reserve MiG-29s Fell Apart
articles.text:
In February 2019, as the Indian Air Force (IAF) grappled with the implications of a shrinking fighter fleet, one attractive bargain awaited at a Russian hangar: 21 MiG-29 airframes, produced in the late 1980’s as a gift to the Soviet Air Force, never paid for, assembled or flown. Their wings were stored separately from their fuselages and collected dust for three decades. India – the first export customer for the MiG-29 – was invited to buy them at a price close to the construction cost: reportedly under $25 million each, cheaper than a Tejas Mk-1.
The IAF was interested. A technical team visited Russia in January 2019 and reported the “skeletion” to be in good condition. Moscow promised to upgrade the jets to the MiG-29UPG standard already in use in India, transforming the 1980’s air-defence interceptor into a modern multi-role fighter. For an air-force needing to maintain a minimum of 30 squadrons against a sanctioned 42, with the retirement of the MiG-21’s and the still distant debut of the LCA Mk-2 and AMCA, a ready-made fourth MiG-29 squadron was attractive.
The deal cleared its biggest hurdle on 2 July 2020, when the Defence Acquisition Council – chaired by Rajnath Singh – approved the purchase of 21 MiG-29 and the upgrade of 59 existing ones for an estimated ₹7,418 crore, as well as the procurement of 12 Su-30MKIs from HAL. It came in the wake of the Ladakh clashes with China, and was portrayed as an urgent need to “strengthen the Armed Forces for the defence of our borders.”
The deal then stalled – and never picked up again. Russia delivered its commercial offer to India in 2021. Then the file lay dormant. The invasion of Russia’s February 2022 of Ukraine proved critical. With Russian banks isolated from the global payments system, the payment mode became open to doubt and questions were raised about Moscow’s ability to deliver. In March 2022, a United States official testified to the Senate that India had cancelled the MiG-29 order; New Delhi said that no formal decision had been taken, but that the deal was essentially frozen. Indian officials blamed the Russian logistical problems, while the government became hesitant to authorise major new Russian purchases.
Even before Russia invaded Ukraine, the MoD had begun its review of “Buy Global” purchases to promote indigenisation. Analysts pointed India was leaning towards cancelling the deal as a part of self-reliance, not as a punishment of Russia.
By September 2023, the outcome of this process was clear. The DAC approved the acquisition of 12 additional Su-30MKIs, while officials admitted the July 2020 proposal “did not materialise” and a modified deal was approved. The 21 MiG-29 were removed from it.
There were flickers of interest. In 2024, reports suggested the MiG-29 acquisition might be re-examized as India and Russia worked out a payment route that bypassed sanctions. But no contract was signed.
The irony is that the need never receded. The IAF still operates three MiG-29UPG squadrons, wants a fourth and even projected an “urgent requirement” to re-arm the type with new stand-off weapons. The 21 jets built for a Soviet order that was never completed would have fitted in perfectly with such a need.
In the end, the jets are an example of how a cheap-looking offer can be undermined by cost escalations, payment politics, and a drift away from Russian hardware – a deal that was less the casualty of any singular decision than a confluence of timing, sanctions and self-reliance all pulling in the same direction.

articles.title: Musk disputes NASA safety panel's lunar launch estimates
articles.text:
NASA's safety watchdog, the Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel (ASAP), had good news and bad news for the space agency, and SpaceX boss Elon Musk quickly disagreed with some of it.

Musk disputed the reported suggestion that approximately 22 launches might be needed to support a landing by the Human Landing System (HLS) variant of Starship on the Moon. "That's way too high," Musk responded on X. "Actual number will be more like 6 to 8."

The US lunar landers being developed for Artemis require refueling in space, meaning additional launches to deliver propellant before astronauts can head to the surface. During Apollo, a single Saturn V launch was enough to send a fully fueled Lunar Module to the Moon.

The problem is demonstrating reliable transfers of cryogenic propellant between spacecraft at the scale these heavier, more complex landers require. Apollo's Lunar Module used hypergolic propellants instead. To date, SpaceX has managed one Starship test flight to orbit. Many more will undoubtedly follow, but if the launch figure cited by the panel is accurate, Musk's rocketeers face a challenging road ahead.

Even with the rescoping that made Artemis III a low Earth orbit demonstration of lunar technologies from Blue Origin and SpaceX in 2027, the Artemis program remains ambitious, particularly considering the desire to get humans on the lunar surface before President Trump leaves office.

ASAP praised Artemis II and NASA's new administrator, Jared Isaacman, but raised concerns about future access to low Earth orbit. SpaceX's plans to phase out Falcon rockets and Dragon spacecraft could complicate any extension of International Space Station (ISS) operations and the launch of its deorbit vehicle.

Then there is Boeing's Calamity Capsule, Starliner. Last month, a possible uncrewed launch date around December 2026 was mooted, but the panel now puts the earliest possible launch in mid-January 2027, with the schedule still under review.

An end to Dragon operations could leave Starliner as the only commercial option for getting astronauts to and from the ISS, not quite the redundancy NASA hoped for, and a stark reminder that commercial businesses aren't required to provide services indefinitely and can change direction when their contracts end.

There is also only one US alternative to the cargo variant of Dragon: Northrop Grumman's Cygnus. An international cargo alternative is JAXA's HTV-X.

Russia continues to carry crews on Soyuz spacecraft and cargo on Progress freighters, but NASA has long sought US alternatives.

A written report is due early next year, doubtless with plenty of observations and recommendations. ®

articles.title: Rafale vs J-16 Debate Sparks Fresh Row in Chinese Media
articles.text:
Chinese military forums have pushed back against Indian media outlets’ coverage of a People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) pilot’s assessment of the Rafale, taking up the issue of close-in manoeuvrability as an opportunity to discuss overall performance and India’s intention to acquire 114 additional combat aircraft.
This issue has gained traction between October 11 and 17 after Chinese state broadcaster CCTV aired an interview with J-16 pilot Wei Yuexin, who spoke about encounters with Egyptian Rafale fighters during the China-Egypt Eagles of Civilization 2026 exercise. His comments acknowledged the advantages of the Rafale in close-range manoeuvrability, a position that Indian defence outlets have interpreted as an assessment of the French fighter’s overall capabilities.
The responses from Chinese military pundits and web forums have stressed the nuance of the pilot’s comments, asserting that a narrow observation on a particular aspect of aerial combat should not be taken as an endorsement of overall PLAAF inferiority.
Among the arguments made on sites such as NetEase, Sohu and Toutiao, the primary counterpoint stressed the difference between visual-range and beyond-visual-range (BVR) combat, and the J-16’s advantages in the latter, including its radar, electronic warfare systems, missiles and the potential for it to operate in tandem with airborne early warning aircraft. However, while the J-16’s BVR capabilities may give it an edge in that particular arena, that does not necessarily offset its possible shortcomings in a one-on-one dogfight, nor does it take into account other factors such as pilot experience, weapons and support systems. Nor have any of the publicly reported exchanges provided enough information on the rules of engagement, or the outcome of the exercises, to determine whether one aircraft has a clear advantage over the other in different combat scenarios.
The argument on both sides of the discussion has also recalled the events of the India-Pakistan air battle of May 2025. The Chinese comments noted that Pakistani J-10CE fighters, armed with PL-15 missiles, had shot down four Indian Rafales. Those claims have not been formally acknowledged by either side of the conflict, and the numbers cited should not be taken as confirmed facts.
The writers also note what they perceive as an attempt by Indian and Western outlets to dismiss Chinese and Pakistani accounts of the 2025 clashes and imply that they were using the CCTV segment to advance their position.
As such, India’s military pundits have applied the comments to the acquisition of MRFA, a requirement for 114 fighters currently under consideration by the IAF. According to a Sohu commentary, India should consider the Eurofighter Typhoon as an option rather than simply Rafale or the F-35, an observation that indicates that the Chinese writers were applying and testing the observations to the acquisition scenario.
For India, the more useful takeaway is the observation that the effectiveness of any particular aircraft or missile depends on the situation and the support it receives. While the CCTV comments may provide some insight into the possible outcome of a particular scenario, neither side has officially released enough information for either to take a firm position on the capabilities of either aircraft in different scenarios.

articles.title: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
articles.text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises

Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?

In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.

Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.

Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!

In the biotech world, you can’t see everything

—Jessica Hamzelou

Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. 

Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. This is why it left me questioning how we cover science.

This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

Help choose our next Roundtables topic

Our subscriber-only Roundtables bring you into conversation with MIT Technology Review editors and reporters. Now, we want your help choosing our next topic: how to keep your mind going for longer, or what it would take to put a city on the moon. Which do you most want to hear about? 

Vote for your preferred topic by Monday at 12 p.m. ET.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Palmer Luckey’s new startup plans to genetically enhance military dogs
Warhound says the dogs will detect explosives and protect troops. (Wired $)
+ It’s raised $200 million from investors, including Sequoia. (TechCrunch)
+ Colossal Biosciences will help clone and gene-edit the dogs. (Bloomberg $)
+ The Pentagon wants an AI-powered lie detector. (MIT Technology Review)

2 Donald Trump says Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s Starlink access
But Zelensky says Starlink speeds remained capped. (Reuters $)

articles.title: IAF Issues RFP for Maintenance of 46 ATCR-33S Radars
articles.text:
The Indian Air Force (IAF) has sent out a request for proposal (RFP) relating to maintenance support for 46 ATCR-33S airfield surveillance radars at its various air bases, with Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) being the one designated to receive the service tender. The aim of the requirement is to ensure radar availability, minimise equipment downtime and provide support for the more recent Mk XII(S) Identification Friend or Foe (IFF) systems.
As the information given shows, the radar fleet consists of ATCR-33S systems that were purchased in 2003, 2007 and 2017. The need for maintenance shows that it is necessary to keep the airfield surveillance infrastructure acquired during various procurement periods operational so that the systems can be used for regular air traffic monitoring and for military flying operations.
A major performance requirement is that the serviceability rate at each location must exceed 95 per cent. This establishes a high standard of availability for the maintenance provider and highlights the importance of preventive maintenance, prompt fault diagnosis, and having replacement parts on hand. The condition at the site level is important since the overall performance of the fleet alone would not show that each air base is meeting the required serviceability standard.
The tender sets out a requirement for a response time of 72 hours in the case of breakdowns and a four-day period for carrying out on-site repairs. The aim of these time limits is to reduce the length of time during which a radar is unavailable after a fault has been reported. Whether these deadlines can be met at the various air bases spread over a wide area will depend on the maintenance organisation’s technical support facilities, its access to spare parts and its capacity to quickly deploy personnel.
The scope also covers maintenance support for the more recent Mk XII(S) IFF systems. Equipment for IFF allows compatible military vehicles and ground-based systems to swap out identification signals, which helps in telling friendly aircraft apart from other radar contacts. Since support for the IFF component is thus a vital element in keeping the overall radar system going, it should be noted that the information provided does not state whether the requirement involves the installation of new hardware, software upgrades or merely the maintenance of the existing equipment.
The fact that BEL is involved is in keeping with the role of Indian defence electronics companies in supporting military radar and communications infrastructure; a structured service agreement would enable the IAF to ensure continuity with respect to its existing radar fleet while dealing with equipment faults and keeping the related systems running.
The fact that maintenance is required also shows how important it is to provide lifecycle support for airfield surveillance equipment. The performance of radar depends not just on the original design of the system but also on continuous maintenance, calibration, the replacement of components and support for the related identification systems. The longer the equipment is in use, the more important it becomes to have reliable access to technical expertise and spare parts.

articles.title: Torvalds: AI is fine for competent devs, but spare us the 'drive-by' patches
articles.text:
Linus Torvalds is embracing AI to write Linux kernel code, and some people are having fits. He has a message for them. So do I.

Roy Schestowitz, editor of Tux Machines, summed up his reaction to the news as "Linus Torvalds Turns to Slop." In the podcast Pivot to AI, podcaster David Gerard agreed: "Linux kernel goes full AI slop code." Meanwhile, in the Tom's Hardware comments section, commenter "LordVile" wrote: "This is a publicity stunt from his AI overlords [The Linux Foundation] who pay his wage." They followed this by saying this is the "same reason he's flipped-flopped on AI."

I've known Linus for a few decades, and I don't take his use of AI as evidence that he's suddenly abandoned his standards. And the very idea that he'd do anything he didn't want to do with Linux on behalf of the Linux Foundation, or anyone else, is ludicrous.

I get it, though. There are reasons to be suspicious of AI. I've written about many of them. For instance, AI model collapse, which happens when AI engines learn from other AI models and their ties to the truth fray. It's a very real problem. Not, mind you, that LLMs find the grist for their answer mills from very reliable sources in the first place.

Even when AI gets good data, as it does in programming, its owners pay little to no attention to the copyrights and licenses protecting the open source code it picked up its coding tricks from. As for paying for the information it runs on, please! The very idea that Big AI must pay writers, artists, you name it, for using their work is anathema to them.

All that said, when it comes to programming, the ship has sailed. AI is becoming part of the programming toolkit, whether its critics like it or not. Why? Because while you still can't vibe code your way into delivering production-quality software, when someone who knows what they're doing, like Torvalds, uses AI, it can be very useful.

Anyone who says otherwise is just making the same mistake the Luddites did. Who now, some of you may ask? They were textile workers who attacked machinery in the early 19th century in protest against changes threatening their wages and livelihoods. You may have noticed that while people still weave cloth by hand, industrial production is mechanized. The same is happening now with AI and programming. I think we're about halfway through the process, and by 2030 or so, people programming by "hand" will be about as common as weavers doing it by hand are today.

In short, get over it. I don't love it, either. I write for a living, and my business is being crunched too. At least in programming, quality work still counts, no matter how it's done. With writing, though, true AI slop is increasingly the rule, not the exception.

Back to Linux: at the Linux Kernel Maintainers Summit in Prague the other week, Sasha Levin, a Linux kernel developer, announced that the maintainers had decided to "deprecate the Assisted-by Tag." That means you no longer need to say if you used AI in your code submissions.

That doesn't mean you can turn in slop, though. That code won't pass muster. As Torvalds told me in a note the other day: "I think the whole 'don't use AI for commit messages' kind of argument … Maybe it's well-intentioned, but I think it's entirely misguided. I really think we want competent people to use AI as a tool."

Competent is the key word there. Torvalds also wrote: "The 'clueless people using AI' problem is different. I do think we want to discourage that. Not discourage the people who use AI and truly want to learn and truly want to become useful members of the kernel community – but discourage the drive-by patches, and discourage people who just want to feel like they sent a patch and never really wanted to become anything more. We all start clueless, but some people spend the time and effort to become something more." Exactly so.

As Torvalds said at Open Source Summit Europe: "I think [vibe-coding is] a wonderful way to find joy in programming. It makes you feel like you're doing something relevant. It allows you, as a new programmer, to do things that you would otherwise have a really hard time with." He added: "I love the concept of AI as a gateway drug" to programming.

Besides, AI has already proven very useful for improving Linux code. As long-term Linux kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman told me back in March: "Months ago, we were getting what we called 'AI slop,' AI-generated security reports that were obviously wrong or low quality." But then, "something happened a month ago, and the world switched. Now we have real reports." It's not just Linux, he continued. "All open source projects have real reports that are made with AI, but they're good, and they're real."

True, the maintainers are getting buried in good bug reports now, but as Kroah-Hartman and discussed in Prague, AI bug finders might eventually exhaust the readily discoverable problems, easing the pressure on maintainers.

Another AI win is that you can use AI to reverse-engineer Windows drivers for Linux more easily. Christian F.K. Schaller, Red Hat's director of software engineering, created hw-harness while working on a Linux driver for a slide scanner. This open source project provides "tooling for working out how a piece of hardware behaves so that you can write a Linux driver for it."

By automating some seriously slow, tedious ways of figuring out what a binary-only driver was doing with the hardware, Schaller has made building Linux drivers from Windows drivers much easier. I know, because I did this myself back in the mid-2000s, and those manual methods are still what people use today. This could go a long way toward fixing one of those lingering annoyances of the Linux desktop: poor or entirely missing hardware drivers.

In the meantime, Torvalds told me: "Well, in all fairness, we do clearly have an 'AI problem.' Or rather, we have two independent AI problems: we have a large codebase that AI finds real bugs in, and that adds a lot of work on already fairly overworked maintainers. And then we have people who use AI to generate patches without actually understanding the code in question."

He continued: "But I'd argue that these aren't problems with AI itself; they are just problems that are exposed by AI. They are very much both very real problems, and I understand that people can really come to dislike – and even hate – AI due to them, but I do think the underlying issue isn't AI itself."

It's how people misuse AI. In the right hands, as the top Linux programmers are showing us, AI can be useful. ®

articles.title: F-35 vs Su-57: Why Former US Pilots Say Su-57 Could Make Sense for India more then F-35
articles.text:
India’s pursuit of a fifth-gen fighter has attracted fresh international interest after ex-US military pilots C.W. Lemoine and T.K. Hartsock discussed the possible acquisition of America’s F-35 Lightning II or Russia’s Su-57 Felon on The Mover and Gonky Show. They discussed the competing considerations for New Delhi, including that of aircraft capability, technology transfer, domestic manufacturing and India’s existing defence relationships.
The discussion followed Indian Air Force Chief Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh’s remarks, following the conclusion of Exercise Tarang Shakti 2026 in Jodhpur, when sitting alongside US Pacific Air Forces commander General Kevin Schneider he joked that American personnel did not even allow Indian officials to approach the F-35, despite reports of a possible sale. He also made clear that the United States had not made a formal offer to sell the aircraft to India.
On the podcast Lemoine, who flies the F-16 and F/A-18, and Hartsock, who has flown the F/A-18 and T-38 considered the practical obstacles to an Indian purchase and discussed the differences between being able to see an aircraft for test and a formal offer, particularly when it involves technology and security arrangements.
Hartsock gave an example of Malaysia considering the F/A-18 Super Hornet and how an aircraft could be configured with software representative of the export version and argued it would be more complicated with the single-seat F-35 because there is no two-seat variation. The discussion was an assessment by the hosts, who were not confirming any arrangement being considered for India.
The two pilots also considered the Russian Su-57 as a potential alternative purchase. The aircraft would be more familiar to India as the Indian Air Force operates the Su-30MKI and has decades of experience with Russian-origin combat aircraft. However, familiarity does not automatically mean that the Su-57 would meet India’s requirements or offer the best value for money.
The argument of the podcast was that the choice would have more than a difference between the performance of the aircraft in the air, but that Russia would be more likely to offer local manufacturing or industrial participation and the hosts questioned whether Washington would be prepared to provide India with access to sensitive technology on the F-35. Neither country’s final terms for a potential Indian acquisition has not yet been discussed.
The hosts also raised China’s rising fifth-gen fighter capabilities and the possibility of Pakistan purchasing the Chinese J-35. They argued that this could influence India’s assessment of what it needs to counter emerging regional threats. However, reports about a potential Pakistani acquisition should not be conflated with confirmed operational deployment.
India’s indigenous Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA) programme adds further complexity. India has to consider if the urgency of getting a stealth aircraft will outweigh the advantages of investing into an indigenous platform that could offer greater control over future upgrades and technology. A foreign acquisition would offer a quicker route into having a fifth-gen aircraft, but could have significant costs and long-term reliance on a foreign supplier.
The Indian Air Force has not selected either aircraft. Air Chief Marshal Singh stated that the Russian Su-57 proposal had come to the service’s attention, but no decision had been made on whether to evaluate it. He said the IAF would assess the aircraft after receiving a government decision.

BOFH: I talked to Claude and he says you're an idiot
articles.text:
Working in the same place for what feels like millennia can have its benefits, however working for the same place for what seems like millennia carrying over all the benefits of your original contract can be even better than that.

Some of those benefits are, admittedly, useless to me. I'm unlikely to avail myself of the Company-reimbursed landline (that all on-call personnel are entitled to), and I won't be needing the 2400bps modem or the VT100 for after hours support. The one month pregnancy leave is also off the cards.

What is in play, however, as the PFY has recently discovered, is accumulated sick leave. It appears that we've been racking up two weeks a year to a point that I now have sufficient sick leave to safely get leprosy.

Obviously, I'm not going to exercise that particular option, but both the PFY and I have been considering roads not taken in recent times...

...

"Ahh... Just, um, following up on your recent, uh, illnesses." The Boss asks uneasily.

"Oh yes?" I ask.

"This, uh, acute bronchitis a few Fridays back."

"Oh yeah, it was terrible," I lie. "Hacking cough, not pleasant at all. I was wheezing like a coal-fired Trabant."

"And that particular illness lasted... a single day?"

"Apparently," I say. "All good now though."

"And Stephen. He had acute... otitis media around the same time."

"The ear thing?" I respond. "Yes, apparently it really affected his balance."

"Okay, fair enough. But then you had acute sinusitis on the Monday? And Stephen had asthma on the Tuesday?"

"Yes, that sounds about right." I nod.

"Then.. Back spasms for you last Friday and campylobacter for Stephen on Monday?"

"I blame myself. I carried a large Vindaloo banquet for six back to work on the Wednesday night. The PFY took the leftovers back home for dinner following day. He's never been great with food hygiene."

"And then I see fibromyalgia for you and food poisoning for Stephen?"

"Yeah, like I said, he's not that great with food hygiene. He tends to follow the five minute rule."

"Hmm. And is there any reason why you seem to be getting sick in... uh... alphabetical order?" the Boss asks.

"It's as much a mystery to you as to me," I admit, making a mental note to vary things a bit. "Illness seems to be attracted to us like a hippy to a salt lamp."

"And, uh, no medical certificate for any of these illnesses?" the Boss enquires.

"I checked with Claude, and he told me that according to my contract I'd only need a med cert for a three-or-more-days illness."

"You have been ill for more than three days. Just yesterday you had conjunctivitis."

"Firstly, I believe it's contiguous sick days, and secondly, the conjunctivitis was so bad it would have been irresponsible to drive to the doctor..."

"And yet your eyesight was sufficient for you to type in questions to Claude?" the Boss asks, astutely.

"Oh no, I spoke to Claude."

It's a bit early to be calling check-mate at this stage, but I have to admit to feeling smug.

"The actual wording of your contract indicates that the conditions can be varied by written notice," the Boss points out.

"And I take it you've written a notice?" I ask, noticing a folded page in the Boss' hand.

The Boss hands the paper to me, still warm from the printer.

"You'll note that it's in writing, signed and dated," the Boss points out.

"Well that's me told," I say, feeling a little like I'll have a dental problem tomorrow.

...two days later...

"And so I'm just after your med cert for your, er, dental abscess," the Boss asks, skipping the niceties.

"Oh yes, right. I spoke to Claude, and he looked over my contract again. Apparently he says that giving me written notice is (a) not retrospective, and that I probably already had the dental issue before you gave me written notice, but also (b) written notice can only vary the contract by mutual agreement."

"And I take it you don't agree?" the Boss asks.

"Claude says I don't. But I got a medical opinion anyway."

… two minutes later..

"An email, apparently from Claude, saying it definitely sounds like you have an abscess is NOT a medical certificate."

"But Claude's a medical expert. He's got access to a vast database of medical information on the web."

"That doesn't count," the Boss snaps.

"Claude says it does," I counter.

"Oh, so Claude's a lawyer as well then?" the Boss snaps sarcastically.

articles.title: UK threatens subsea cable saboteurs with 14 years behind bars
articles.text:
Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of keeping Russian submarines away from critical infrastructure.

The government on Thursday set out plans to overhaul legislation dating back to 1885 and introduce tougher penalties for damaging the underwater cables and pipelines that keep Britain's internet and energy supplies running.

According to Whitehall, subsea cables carry around 99 percent of the UK's international data traffic, while underwater pipelines account for 74 percent of its gas supply. Yet much of this infrastructure is protected by laws written when the telegraph was cutting-edge technology.

The Submarine Telegraph Act 1885 originally imposed a £100 maximum fine for damaging a cable through culpable negligence. That might have been a reasonable deterrent back then, but it's unlikely to give today's would-be saboteurs much pause.

Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical subsea energy or telecoms infrastructure could face up to 14 years behind bars. The proposals also set tougher penalties, including unlimited fines, for reckless or negligent damage.

Subsea telecoms operators would face new legal duties to identify and manage security risks, while ministers would gain powers to direct companies and cable repair providers to take action where necessary and proportionate to protect national security.

The government also wants to regulate fiber-optic sensing technology, which uses subsea cables to detect activity at sea but could pose a security risk if sensitive data falls into hostile hands.

Unsurprisingly, Russia features prominently in Whitehall's thinking.

In April, British forces exposed a covert Russian submarine operation near critical undersea infrastructure. The operation reportedly involved an attack submarine acting as a decoy while two specialist vessels surveyed Britain's cable routes.

"The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure, yet some of the laws protecting these vital connections date back more than a century," said telecoms minister Ian Murray.

The plans aren't entirely new. In May, the government announced its intention to toughen penalties and introduce security obligations for cable operators. Thursday's White Paper spells out the proposed penalties and how far ministers could go in directing operators to act.

It also follows warnings from Parliament's Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, which concluded last year that Britain was insufficiently prepared for a coordinated attack on its subsea infrastructure. MPs and peers warned that government assessments focused too heavily on individual cable failures, rather than what might happen if attackers simultaneously targeted connections to Europe and across the Atlantic.

Russian submarines aren't responsible for every severed cable. Fishing boats and ships dragging their anchors do most of the damage, accounting for up to 97 percent of faults, according to previous government estimates.

And even when sabotage is suspected, catching those responsible is another matter. Britain already has laws allowing life sentences for serious acts of state-backed sabotage, but they're not much use if nobody can prove who did it. That's rather difficult when the crime scene is at the bottom of the sea. And it might prove equally difficult to extradite suspects from enemy nation states.

None of this is law yet. The government has opened a 12-week consultation on the plans, after which ministers will decide how to proceed.

Whether the threat of a lengthy prison sentence will trouble Russian submariners is debatable. Even so, after 140 years, Britain's subsea cable laws are finally getting dragged out of the Victorian era. ®

articles.title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
articles.text:
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes. 

I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.

Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.

In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.

Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.

Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.

Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.

In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.

It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.

As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?

I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?

But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.

I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?

One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.

Except that sometimes you can’t.

Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.

At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.

I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?

I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim. 

But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!

This article first appeared in The Checkup, MIT Technology Review’s weekly biotech newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Thursday, and read articles like this first, sign up here.

articles.title: Beware the claw: Do you want to win the bunny or reboot Android?
articles.text:
Today's victim of the bork fairy is a claw machine that even Android seems to have rejected for its alleged unfairness. And Google, as we all know, is all about fairness.

Eagle-eyed Register reader Scott spotted the stricken machine in an arcade adjacent to a roller rink, a place our reader visited with a friend and described as "something my currently bruised body reminds me I hadn't done for about 20 years."

We assume they were talking about roller-skating, and not the exertions of accompanying their pal.

The machine itself is a recent iteration of the infamous claw machine, which has spent a century emptying players' pockets in exchange for frustration and the very occasional reward of tat. Infamously, the devices are sometimes rigged so the claw's strength varies between turns, and in several parts of the world, gambling laws cover the machines.

However, the only gambling to be done here is on whether or not Android will boot. Like so many players in the past, the machine has lost this bet, and an Android Recovery Console is on show. We're not sure who lennie022 is – perhaps a user or perhaps some corporate account – but the words "release-keys" probably don't belong on top of the device. They're unlikely to entice any everyday players to part with cash.

The usual recovery menu is hidden thanks to the dimensions of the screen. If something like this comes up on a mobile device, the volume up and down buttons tend to be used for navigation. In this case, the joystick is presumably the only I/O method, and the selected option would be pot-luck. Which, we guess, is the whole point.

More discreet is the screen below the machine which, rather than encourage a player to grip the sweaty handle, is now plaintively asking for some removable storage (we've seen enough electronic gizmos to know what those pictograms mean) on a blue background that would bring a tear to the eye of many a Microsoft engineer.

In fact, something that looks a bit like a blue screen of death and a borked Android? Perhaps this combination would lure an engineer to the controls… Sure, there's no obvious place to stick removable storage or attach a keyboard. But a waggle of the joystick couldn't hurt, could it? Perhaps one more?

Dammit. Now we're restarting Android, when all we wanted was that pink bunny. ®

articles.title: Vendor-affiliated AI agent tech gets adopted by friendly, funded foundation
articles.text:
The Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) has been entrusted with stewardship of four additional AI projects in the hope of broadening the set of vendor-neutral tools for making AI agents.

The AAIF was founded in December 2025 under the auspices of the Linux Foundation as a vendor-neutral organization for the benefit of AI companies more interested in riding a tide that lifts all boats than making waves.

It launched with three projects under its supervision: Model Context Protocol (MCP), goose, and AGENTS.md. With the four new adoptees, there are now 10 projects sheltering under the AAIF's wings.

The donor organizations – Alibaba, Anthropic, Hugging Face, and OpenAI – have handed over control of OpenSandbox, Agent Skills, OpenEnv, and Open Responses respectively.

Each of these projects provides functions that developers of AI agents – which typically combine models, tools, and a task loop – may find helpful. And having a more or less agreed-upon blueprint for implementation tends to make deployment easier and more predictable, at least until your AI agent unexpectedly ransacks some third-party organization.

OpenSandbox provides a way to constrain or sandbox the capabilities of AI agents using various client SDKs, tools, protocols, lifecycle hooks, container runtimes, and assorted in-sandbox execution components.

Agent Skills outlines a format for text descriptions that guide AI agents through specified tasks more effectively. It provides context that helps agents accomplish their goals.

"We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral," said Anthropic, an AAIF co-founder, in a blog post.

OpenEnv offers a containerized service for creating reinforcement learning environments that can be built without much trouble, can interoperate, and can scale to meet demanding testing.

And Open Responses is an open API specification for building LLM interfaces that can work with different model providers. It standardizes common request and response formats, streaming events, and tool invocation patterns.

The AAIF's nurturing of these technical specs has attracted considerable interest from companies convinced that there's a future in AI agents. The organization has surpassed 300 members in less than a year, with 60 coming on board this quarter, including Ant Group, Gates Foundation, MongoDB, Nutanix, Royal Bank of Canada, Vercel, and Vultr as Gold Members.

This enthusiastic (or credulous) embrace of AI agents may be a bit too rapid for some industries. Axios is reporting that US banks have become concerned that AI agents are interacting with customer accounts without bank authorization (though not necessarily without customer authorization). ®

articles.title: Windows said modem worked fine. That unmistakable scorched electronics smell suggested otherwise
articles.text:
Energy can be hard to find on Friday mornings, which is why The Register uses them to offer a fresh instalment of On Call – the reader-contributed column that shares your hopefully empowering tech support stories.

This week, meet a reader we’ll Regomize as “Lachlan,” who told us he once did tech support for a senior exec who had a side hustle writing essays for Japanese university students attending UK universities.

The exec asked Lachlan for help diagnosing a sudden inability to send or receive email, an obvious hindrance to the side hustle.

This story took place in the dialup age, so Lachlan sensibly assumed that the exec’s modem was misbehaving.

“I checked the network settings, nothing wrong there,” he told On Call. Next, he checked the cables, and if the line the modem used had a dial tone. Again, all was well.

“At this point I decided to make sure the device was correctly installed in Windows Device Manager,” Lachlan wrote. “I had a lot of experience in the dark arts of serial communications and there was an option in the advanced settings in Device Manager to send a series of low level AT commands to the modem, which would return responses.”

He ran the tests, and Windows reported that the modem was in the pink of health.

With all that done, Lachlan decided the time had come to replace the modem.

“When I opened the PC, I got a faint whiff of that unmistakable scorched PCB smell,” he wrote. “By looking at the modem you couldn’t normally see if any of the chips were faulty. In this case there was a black soot mark in the shape of the voltage regulator chip which sits between the phone line and the sensitive chips on the modem.”

“This was to protect the device from the 70V line voltage BT used to create a phone connection,” he explained. “However, in this instance the chip had been vaporized. That wasn’t just a slight over voltage – this was way higher.”

Lachlan asked the exec when his email had stopped working, and if he could recall any recent electrical storms.

He replied by saying his email stopped working while he watched a really impressive display of lightning.

“That voltage regulator chip sacrificed itself for the greater good,” Lachlan wrote.

Has Windows failed to find an obvious fault? Or has lightning lightened your load? In either case, click here to send your story to On Call so we can electrify your fellow readers on a future Friday. ®

articles.title: ShIOEnv: A Command Evaluation Environment for Grammar-Constrained Synthesis and Execution Behavior Modeling
articles.text:
arXiv:2505.18374v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We introduce ShIOEnv, a Gymnasium-compatible Bash environment for synthesizing execution-annotated shell input traces. Datasets containing such traces are useful for training models to perform execution-free shell simulation, which in turn is useful for deploying honeypots for cyber deception. Existing datasets, such as NL2CMD and other Bash command corpora, do not include complete execution artifacts (stdout, stderr, exit status, and changes to the system's state) associated with a command's execution. ShIOEnv synthesizes shell inputs, executes them in a controlled system context, and records stdout, stderr, exit status, and structured filesystem and environment patches. Unconstrained (random) generation of shell inputs (command and arguments) results in multiple instances of arguments that are mostly redundant or result in execution errors. We introduce grammar-constrained synthesis to generate syntactically valid arguments with high input irreducibility, which we estimate through self-ablative contrasts of execution artifacts. We prepare 1.6M samples using grammar-constrained and unconstrained synthesis and collect their execution artifacts for 86 Linux/Bash utilities. Using this dataset, we train small language models (CodeT5) and evaluate their accuracy in predicting the actual execution behavior of attacker-sourced Bash commands. These models outperform commonly used rule-based simulation (Cowrie) and prompted large language models by up to 14.2 pp in output edit similarity (O-ES). We enhance the NL2CMD dataset by constructing 500K samples executable in a grounded system context along with their complete execution artifacts. We empirically demonstrate that models trained on grammar-constrained samples outperform those trained on NL2CMD samples by 22.5 pp in O-ES. ShIOEnv, command grammars, and 2.1M samples used in our primary evaluations are released for use by other researchers.
